1.open: Who is someone who showed up for you at a hard time, even in a small way?
questions: The chapter opens with a famine, a move to a foreign land, and then three deaths in a row (vv. 1-5). If you were in Naomi's place, what do you think you would be feeling by the end of verse 5?

Naomi tells her daughters-in-law, "May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me" (v. 8). What does it say about Naomi that she blesses them while she is grieving herself?
In that world a widow with no sons had no one to provide for her. Why do you think Naomi urges Ruth and Orpah to go home (vv. 11-13)? Was she being unkind, or caring?
Orpah goes back and Ruth "clung to her" (v. 14). The story does not blame Orpah. How do you think we should think about people who feel they can't stay?
Ruth says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (v. 16). What do you think it cost her to say that? Who has made a costly commitment to you, or to someone you know?

Naomi says, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me" (v. 20). The text lets her say this without correcting her. What do you make of a Bible that records such honest complaint?

Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (v. 21). If you have ever felt empty, or unsure where God is, what has that been like? You can answer honestly, even if the answer is mixed.
The chapter ends with the women arriving "at the beginning of the barley harvest" (v. 22). What do you notice about that small detail, and what might it hint at?
1.life: Think of one person who is grieving or going through a hard stretch. This week, show up for them in a simple, practical way, such as a meal, a call or a visit, without trying to fix anything or explain their pain.
1.prayer: Thank God for the people who have stayed with you in hard times. Ask for honesty to bring your own bitterness or emptiness to him, and for care for anyone in the group who is grieving.
1.tip: Naomi blames God, and some people will be uneasy or want to correct her. Let her complaint stand, as the text does, and point out that her grief is heard and that Ruth stays beside her. Also, Christians differ on whether the family's move to Moab and the deaths are meant as a judgment or are simply told as tragedy, so say that briefly and keep the focus on loss and loyalty.

2.open: Think of a time someone unexpectedly went out of their way to be kind to you. What did they do?
questions: Ruth asks to glean "after someone in whose sight I may find favor" (v. 2). What does it tell you that she, a poor foreign widow, goes out to ask for help instead of waiting for it?

The story says Ruth "happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz" (v. 3). Many readers see a quiet hint that God is guiding events. Have you ever looked back and wondered whether something that seemed like chance was more than that?

Boaz greets his workers with "The LORD be with you," and they answer, "The LORD bless you" (v. 4). What does that tell you about the kind of workplace he runs, and what would it look like to bring that spirit into ours?

Boaz tells Ruth to stay close to his servant girls and says, "I have ordered the young men not to touch you" (v. 9). Why does that kind of protection matter so much, and who around us needs someone to look out for them?

Ruth falls on her face and asks, "Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?" (v. 10). When have you felt like an outsider? What did it mean when someone noticed you?

Boaz says Ruth has taken refuge under the wings of "the LORD, the God of Israel" (v. 12), and then he becomes part of the answer to his own blessing. How might God use ordinary people to care for others in the way this verse describes?
Boaz quietly has extra stalks left for her and tells his workers, "Do not rebuke her" (vv. 15-16). Why might helping someone without shaming them matter as much as the help itself?

Naomi, who had been bitter, now speaks of the LORD's "kindness" and calls Boaz a kinsman-redeemer (v. 20). If you are in a place where hope feels thin, what small sign of kindness could you name from the past few weeks, even a tiny one?
2.life: This week, look for one person who is on the edge of your workplace, church, school or neighborhood, and do one quiet, practical kindness for them without drawing attention to it.
2.prayer: Thank God for the people who have shown you kindness when you did not expect it. Ask for open eyes to notice someone who needs welcome and protection this week.
2.tip: Questions 2 and 8 may bring out different views on how God works through events, and some may be unsure. Welcome honest answers, including doubt. Also note that Christians differ on whether Boaz is mainly a picture of Jesus or mainly an example of faithful kindness, and many hold both, so you do not need to settle it.

3.open: Who is someone you would call if you were in real trouble, and what makes them easy to ask?
questions: Naomi says, "should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?" (v. 1). What do you think Naomi is worried about, and what does her plan show about how she cares for Ruth?
Ruth answers, "I will do everything you say" (v. 5). When have you trusted someone older or wiser enough to follow their advice, even when it felt risky?

In verse 9 Ruth asks Boaz to "spread the corner of your garment over me," because he is a kinsman-redeemer. In the world of the story, a redeemer was a relative who rescued family in trouble. Who has played that role for you, or who might you play it for?

Christians read the night scene in different ways. Some see an innocent appeal that followed local custom, and others see a risky and morally complex moment. What do you notice in the text itself, and how comfortable are you leaving some of it uncertain?
Boaz says Ruth has "shown more kindness now than before" and is "a woman of noble character" (vv. 10, 11). What does he seem to value in her, and why might that matter more than what she offers him?
Boaz admits that "there is a redeemer nearer than I" and promises to do the right thing either way (v. 12). Why might it matter that he does not take a shortcut, even when he could?

Naomi once came home bitter and empty. Now Boaz says, "Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed" (v. 17). Where have you seen God or other people fill an empty place in your life, even in a small way?
Naomi tells Ruth, "Wait, my daughter," until "you find out how things go" (v. 18). What are you waiting on right now, and what makes the waiting hard? It is fine to say you are not sure God is in it.
3.life: Think of one person you have been afraid to ask for help. This week, ask them, and say plainly what you need. If you are the one others turn to, look for a quiet way to make it safe for someone to ask you.
3.prayer: Thank God for the people who have stood by you when you had nothing to offer. Ask for honesty to ask for help, and for patience in whatever you are waiting on.
3.tip: The night scene on the threshing floor is where the group will likely stall or snicker. Say once, calmly, that Christians read it differently, and note that the text shows Boaz acting honorably and protecting Ruth's name. Then steer back to the themes of risk, kindness and waiting.

4.open: Who is someone who showed up for you or your family when you really needed help?
questions: Boaz takes the matter to the town gate and gathers ten elders as witnesses (vv. 1-2). Why might it matter that this was settled openly and not in private?

Boaz tells the closer relative, "If you want to redeem it, do so" (v. 4). Then the man backs out once he learns Ruth comes with the land (vv. 5-6). What do you think was going on in his mind? Have you ever backed away from helping when you saw what it would cost?
The relative says he "cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance" (v. 6). What are the modern versions of that worry when we are asked to give time, money or comfort?
Boaz says Ruth is "the Moabitess" and still takes her as his wife (v. 10). In that world she was a foreigner and a widow with no standing. What does his choice say about how he sees people?
The people at the gate bless Ruth and say she will be like Rachel and Leah, who "built up the house of Israel" (v. 11). What do you notice about how the community welcomes her?

Earlier in the book Naomi felt empty and bitter. Now the women say, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer" (v. 14). If you have come through a hard stretch, or are still in one, where have you seen help arrive, or where are you finding it hard to see?

The women say Ruth "is better to you than seven sons" (v. 15). Ruth was ordinary and an outsider, yet she mattered a great deal. Who in your life is easy to overlook but has quietly held things together?
The chapter ends with a family list leading to David (vv. 17-22). Why might the writer want us to know that a foreign widow's story is part of Israel's greatest story?
4.life: Think of one person who is alone or struggling, like Naomi and Ruth at the start. This week, do one costly, practical thing for them, such as a meal, a ride, a visit or a phone call that you would normally put off.
4.prayer: Thank God for the people who have stood by you when it cost them something. Ask for open eyes to see who needs help, and for willingness to give it.
4.tip: Some readers see Boaz mainly as a picture of Jesus our redeemer, and others read the chapter as a human story of loyalty and kindness leading to David. Say that plainly in one line, then let the group stay with what Boaz actually does. Also be gentle with the unnamed relative; his choice is understandable, so avoid making him a villain.
